summary: Updates the ASN.1 modules for the PKIX certificate format and related formats from the 1988 to the 2002 version of ASN.1. Nothing changes on the wire; only the syntax used to describe them is brought up to date. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5912 rewrites the way PKIX certificates and related formats are described using modern ASN.1 syntax. The actual certificates on the wire remain exactly the same.

questions: what changed from 1988 asn.1 to 2002 asn.1
subtitle: The PKIX certificate formats rewritten in the 2002 version of ASN.1, with identical bits on the wire.

tldr.problem: Most PKIX-related security RFCs used the deprecated 1988 version of ASN.1 notation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5912 republishes the ASN.1 modules for PKIX RFCs in 2002 ASN.1 syntax, using objects instead of ANY holes, with two new shared modules.
tldr.outcome: The wire encoding does not change. This is an Informational RFC, updated by RFC 6960, RFC 9480 and RFC 9810.

today: RFC 5912 is an Informational RFC that has been updated by RFC 6960, RFC 9480 and RFC 9810.

sections.title: Why New ASN.1 Modules
sections.content:
Many IETF security standards, especially those for PKIX, CMS and S/MIME, were written in the deprecated 1988 version of ASN.1. This document updates the ASN.1 modules to conform to the 2002 version of ASN.1.

It explicitly states there are no bits-on-the-wire changes to any of the formats. The change is only to the notation used to describe them.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like rewriting an old recipe in a newer, clearer format. The result you get is identical, just described differently.

sections.title: Which RFCs Are Covered
sections.content: The document provides updated modules for a set of PKIX-related RFCs, including RFC 2560 (OCSP), RFC 2986 (PKCS #10), RFC 3279 (algorithms), RFC 3852 (attribute certificates v1), RFC 4055 (RSA algorithms), RFC 4210 (CMP), RFC 4211 (CRMF), RFC 5055 (SCVP), RFC 5272 (CMC), RFC 5280 (certificate and CRL profile), and RFC 5755 (attribute certificates v2). The companion RFC 5911 covers CMS and S/MIME.
sections.plainLanguage: The update touches many certificate-related standards, all together in one document.

sections.title: Object Model and Naming Prefixes
sections.content:
The modules use the 2002 ASN.1 object model. Where the 1988 syntax used ANY holes for extensible syntax, the 2002 modules use objects instead. Each algorithm type has its own object set.

Short prefixes indicate the kind of object: id-sha1 is the OID, while mda-sha1 is the message digest object for SHA-1. Examples of prefixes include mda- (message digest), sa- (signature), pk- (public key), cea- (content encryption), and others. When modules share set names, imports disambiguate them.
sections.plainLanguage: Things are named more clearly now: each type of object gets a short tag so it is easy to tell what it is.

sections.title: Shared Modules
sections.content:
Two new modules are introduced: PKIX-CommonTypes and AlgorithmInformation. These hold common definitions used throughout this document and in RFC 5911.

PKIX-CommonTypes defines shared constructs like the ATTRIBUTE and EXTENSION classes, AttributeSet, SingleAttribute, and Extensions. AlgorithmInformation defines classes for digest, signature, key transport, key agreement, key wrap, key derivation, MAC, public key, and content encryption algorithms.

The goal is for these modules to be self-contained where possible, without unnecessary imports.
sections.plainLanguage: Two shared toolboxes are defined so all the other modules can pull from the same set of building blocks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document itself has no security considerations beyond noting the change is purely syntactic. The ASN.1 modules produce identical bits on the wire as the modules they replace.
sections.plainLanguage: Since the actual encoded certificates stay the same, there are no new security risks from this change.
